content: The Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE-USA) is an accrediting body responsible for evaluating and accrediting programs and institutions that offer the Doctor of Chiropractic degree. Its accreditations are officially recognized by the U.S. Department of Education. During the 1920s, there was significant debate within the chiropractic profession regarding the quality of education. This debate primarily involved two organizations: the Universal Chiropractic Association (UCA) and the American Chiropractic Association (ACA). In 1930, these two groups merged to form the National Chiropractic Association (NCA). By 1935, Dr. John Nugent, a chiropractor who had been instrumental in developing the Basic Science Board for healthcare providers, became the first Director of the Committee on Education Standards (CES). Under his leadership, initiatives were undertaken to improve chiropractic education, which eventually led to the establishment of what is now the CCE. Between 1935 and 1940, several national chiropractic organizations, including the NCA, the Chiropractic Health Bureau (CHB), and the Council on State Chiropractic Examining Boards (CSCEB), collaborated to enhance the standards of chiropractic education. During this period, the NCA evolved into the modern American Chiropractic Association (ACA), while the Chiropractic Health Bureau became the International Chiropractors Association (ICA). In 1938, the CES and CSCEB merged to form a new CES, which began conducting institutional self-studies. A questionnaire was distributed to all 37 chiropractic schools in the United States that were actively providing chiropractic education at the time. By 1941, after thorough inspections and evaluations of these institutions, the CES published its first list of schools with provisional approval. Out of the 37 institutions, only 12 were granted provisional approval. Subsequently, the Council on Education (COE) was established, consisting of representatives from these institutions and members of the CES. On August 4, 1947, the COE received formal approval and support from the NCA’s House of Delegates. From 1941 to 1961, the COE worked diligently to improve chiropractic education. This included merging weaker institutions with stronger ones to create more robust academic programs and closing schools that failed to meet minimum standards. By 1961, the number of chiropractic schools in the United States had been reduced from the original 37 to just 10 institutions. In 1964, the NCA merged with other groups to form the current ACA, which continued to support the COE. In 1971, the COE was officially incorporated as the Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE), becoming an independent national organization separate from the ACA. The CCE was first recognized as a Nationally Recognized Accrediting Agency by the U.S. Commissioner of Education in 1974, a status it has maintained ever since. In 1975, the CCE became a member of the Council of Specialized Accrediting Agencies. It was also recognized by the Council on Postsecondary Accreditation (COPA) from 1978 to 1992. In 1992, the CCE received continued recognition from the Council on Recognition of Postsecondary Education (CORPA) for a five-year period, which was subsequently extended until 2002. Today, the CCE is recognized by the Council on Higher Education Accreditation (CHEA), its current accrediting authority.
